# Education in Norway
Organized education in Norway dates back to 2000 B.C., with cathedral schools established following the country becoming an archdiocese in 1153. After the Reformation in 1537 and unification with Denmark, cathedral schools were transformed into Latin schools, and mandatory reading training was introduced in 1736. Norwegian primary education evolved with the folkeskole (people's school), introduced in 1827 and made compulsory for seven years in 1889 and extended to nine years in 1969. The folkeskole was later replaced by the grunnskole (foundation school) in the 1970s and 1980s. The 2003 Independent Schools Act allowed private schooling under strict government approval but such schools remain few and heavily regulated.
Norway’s current school system is divided into three parts: elementary school (barneskole, ages 6–12), lower secondary school (ungdomsskole, ages 13–16), and upper secondary school (videregående skole, ages 16–19). Elementary and lower secondary schooling is compulsory for all children aged 6–16 and together called grunnskole. Students begin with play-based learning and unofficial evaluations at primary level, while formal grading starts in lower secondary. Upper secondary education offers general academic or vocational paths, with many students completing a 2+2 model involving two years of school-based learning followed by apprenticeship. Norway predominantly has public schools, although limited private options exist. The upper secondary graduation rate stood at 73% in 2017.
Higher education in Norway includes universities, university colleges, and private institutions, requiring general university admission certification obtained through upper secondary education or equivalent. Universities focus on theoretical disciplines and awarding bachelor’s, master’s, and doctoral degrees. University colleges also offer professional and engineering degrees and require accreditation for advanced studies. The system allows multiple grading scales, with the Bologna process integrated at tertiary levels. Norway emphasizes inclusive education, with special education typically integrated in local schools and support services available for students with disabilities. The academic year is divided into two semesters from mid-August to June, complemented by national holidays and school breaks.
